# What is this sequence?

Open `data/sequences/mystery_fillet_1.fasta` and see how little the file tells
you. It holds 649 bases of DNA under a header that reads `mystery_fillet_1` and
nothing else. No species, no gene, no date. You can read every base in that file
and still not name the animal it came out of. Naming it is the question this
chapter answers. It's also the question somebody answers every time they check
whether the fish on the label is the fish in the packet.

## Comparing one sequence against everything anyone has deposited

Nobody can reason from 649 bases to a species. What you can do is ask whether
anyone has ever deposited a sequence like this one, and then read what they
called it.

That's the idea behind [BLAST]{.term def="Basic Local Alignment Search Tool. It
takes one sequence and finds the deposited sequences that resemble it, region
by region."}. You hand it one sequence, which is called the *query*. It works
through a pile of deposited sequences and hands back the ones that resemble
your query, ranked, with a score on each.

The pile is the part that's hard to picture. Every report names the database it
went through, and this chapter's search went through this one:

``` {.default .output}
Database: Core nucleotide BLAST database
           128,547,243 sequences; 948,086,538,397 total letters
```

A hundred and twenty-eight million sequences. Nearly a trillion letters, put
there by other people since 1982, none of whom was thinking about your packet.
You don't have to be the first person to sequence this animal. Somebody has to
have got there first and written down what it was.

### Why the find box can't do this

Your browser's find box asks one question: is this exact string present,
character for character. Biology almost never answers yes. Exercise 5.2 sent you
after two versions of *BRCA1*, and the human one, `NM_007294.4`, is 7,088 bases
against 6,648 for the mouse one, `NM_009764.3`. Same gene, same job. The
lengths alone differ by 7,088 − 6,648 = 440 bases, before you count the
mismatches scattered through the stretch they do share. Search for either
sequence inside the other, character for character, and you get nothing. You'd
get nothing for two sequences with no relationship either, so an exact search
can't tell those two situations apart.

BLAST scores instead of matching. It hunts for stretches where two sequences
line up well, tolerates mismatches and gaps inside a stretch, and puts a number
on how good the alignment is. A near-match still scores, which is the
difference that makes the tool work at all.

Here's the part that sounds like a contradiction. The nucleotide search gets
started by exact matching. It chops your query into short words and finds
database sequences carrying one of those words exactly. Then it extends outward
from each one, base by base, keeping score as it goes. A stretch that keeps
scoring gets reported and a stretch that falls apart gets abandoned. Exact
matching is the way in, and scoring is what happens after. The short words also
explain the speed. BLAST looks them up in an index, the way a book's index finds
you a page without reading the book. That's why nearly a trillion letters is
something you wait for rather than something you schedule.

Notice the word *local* in the name. BLAST will line up your 649 bases against
649 bases buried in the middle of a 16,572-base mitochondrial genome and ignore
the rest of that genome entirely. A query doesn't have to be the same kind of
thing as the record it matches, or the same length, or anywhere near it.

<!-- nlr-allow: 16572 -->

### Three programs, and how you pick one

Which BLAST you want comes down to what your query is made of and what you want
to compare it against.

| Your query is | You want hits from | Use |
|---|---|---|
| DNA or RNA | nucleotide records | `blastn` |
| protein | protein records | `blastp` |
| DNA or RNA | protein records | `blastx` |

`blastx` translates your nucleotide query into protein and searches with the
translation. Reach for it when you have a piece of DNA and you care what it
makes rather than which organism it sits in. There are more BLAST programs than
these three. The extra ones move the translation over to the database side of
the comparison, or do it on both sides at once.

`mystery_fillet_1` is DNA, and I want other people's DNA records. So, `blastn`.

You'll put *BRCA1* through this same form in Chapter 7, where each column of the
hit table gets a page. A shorter query with one clear answer is the better thing
to learn the form on, so it goes first.

## Walkthrough: what `mystery_fillet_1` is

Open `blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov` and pick the nucleotide search. Paste the whole
file into the query box, header line and all. Choose the database that covers
nucleotide records generally, rather than one restricted to a single organism.
Then press the button that starts the search.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI BLAST interface on 2 August 2026. NCBI has
redesigned this form more than once and the labels move. Three things are on it
under some name: the box you paste the query into, the menu where you choose
the database, and the button that starts the search. Find those three and the
rest of the layout can move without costing you anything.
:::

The search doesn't run in your browser. It runs on NCBI's machines, in a queue,
behind everybody else's search, which is why the page sits there reloading
itself. Every job gets a request ID, printed at the top of the report as `RID`:

``` {.default .output}
RID: 6Z2TVR6D014

Database: Core nucleotide BLAST database
           128,547,243 sequences; 948,086,538,397 total letters
Query= mystery_fillet_1

Length=649
```

::: {.check}
Read `Length=649` before you read anything else. It matches the file, so the
whole query arrived. A shorter number means the paste got cut off and every
result below it is a search for a fragment you didn't mean to send.
:::

Then the hits. Here are the first twelve rows, with the descriptions trimmed to
fit this page:

``` {.default .output}
                                                           Score     E     Max
Sequences producing significant alignments:                (Bits)  Value  Ident
AB182303.1 Gadus chalcogrammus mitochondrial DNA, comp...  1199    0.0    100%
PZ291804.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher USNM:FISH:48576...  1199    0.0    100%
OL494247.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher H90 cytochrome ...  1199    0.0    100%
FJ165432.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher TZ05-FROSTI-171...  1199    0.0    100%
AM489719.1 Theragra finnmarchica complete mitochondria...  1199    0.0    100%
PZ284884.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher USNM:FISH:48576...  1199    0.0    100%
AB182302.1 Gadus chalcogrammus mitochondrial DNA, comp...  1199    0.0    100%
KX119441.1 Gadus chalcogrammus isolate 61 cytochrome c...  1199    0.0    100%
OL494334.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher H332 cytochrome...  1199    0.0    100%
MN879772.1 Gadus chalcogrammus cytochrome c oxidase su...  1199    0.0    100%
MN850428.1 Gadus chalcogrammus isolate S1 cytochrome c...  1199    0.0    100%
MH035600.1 Gadus chalcogrammus voucher UW151990_5 mito...  1199    0.0    100%
```

Every report in this chapter was run with the hit list capped at fifty rows.
Your own run will probably come back longer, because the form's default cap is
higher than that. A longer list doesn't change the reading. What you count is
how many rows agree with each other, and the length of the list is a display
setting.

Three number columns, and Chapter 7 spends a page on each of them. Here's the
short version. The bit score measures how good the alignment is. The E value
counts how many alignments this good you'd expect to stumble across by
accident. Max Ident is the percentage of aligned positions where the two
sequences carry the same base, rounded to a whole number. Seventeen of these
fifty rows print as 100% and are really 648 of 649.

The names in the left column are doing the work here. `Gadus chalcogrammus` is
Alaska pollock. All fifty rows of this report land in the same genus, on records
deposited by different people from different fish.

Open any one of those rows and you get the alignment it's reporting:

``` {.default .output}
>AB182303.1 Gadus chalcogrammus mitochondrial DNA, complete genome, haplotype:J4
Length=16572

 Score = 1199 bits (649),  Expect = 0.0
 Identities = 649/649 (100%), Gaps = 0/649 (0%)
 Strand=Plus/Plus

Query  1     CCTTTATCTCGTATTTGGTGCCTGAGCCGGCATAGTCGGAACAGCCCTAAGCCTGCTCAT  60
             ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
Sbjct  5495  CCTTTATCTCGTATTTGGTGCCTGAGCCGGCATAGTCGGAACAGCCCTAAGCCTGCTCAT  5554
```

`Query` is your sequence and `Sbjct` is the deposited one, which BLAST calls
the subject. Base 1 of the query sits against base 5,495 of a complete
mitochondrial genome, and the vertical bars mark the positions where the two
agree. The fraction behind that rounded percentage is on the line reading
`Identities = 649/649`. On this row every one of the 649 positions agrees.

<!-- nlr-allow: 5495 -->

Those 649 bases come from one mitochondrial gene: cytochrome c oxidase subunit
I, which everybody shortens to COI.

::: {.why}
Paul D. N. Hebert and colleagues proposed in 2003 that one stretch of COI could
work as an identification tag for animal species. The premise is that COI
differs enough between two species to separate them, and little enough within
one species that two individuals still match. People have been depositing COI
records on purpose ever since, which is why this search filled its whole hit
list with one genus instead of coming back empty.
:::

### One row disagrees with the other forty-nine

Row five says `Theragra finnmarchica`. Different genus, different species, and
it matched all 649 bases exactly.

Theragra got folded into *Gadus*. Whoever deposited `AM489719.1` used the name
that was current on the day they deposited it, and the free-text title on the
record still carries that name. NCBI's taxonomy has since moved on: ask it
which species that record belongs to now and it answers `Gadus finnmarchicus`.
The title is frozen at deposition. The taxonomy behind it is maintained. On
this record the two disagree, and nothing on the page flags it.

So a species name on a record is somebody's opinion, written down on the day
they submitted the sequence. Some of those opinions are decades old. The count
is what carries the answer here. Read the voucher and isolate codes in the
twelve rows above: they come from separate collections, so this isn't one
submitter's mistake copied fifty times.

::: {.trap}
The top row is no more right than the twenty-six under it. Twenty-seven rows in
this report tie at 1199 bits with 649 of 649 identities. Any of the twenty-seven
could have been printed first, and the order among tied rows says nothing about
your fish. Copy the species off row one and stop, and you've copied a name out
of a tie.
:::

<!-- nlr-allow: 1199 -->

### The other fish

Now do the comparison the label invites. The file
`data/sequences/cod_reference_MT456169.fasta` holds a real Atlantic cod
barcode, 655 bases taken off a voucher specimen in a museum collection. Push it
through the same form and every row that comes back is *Gadus morhua*. The top
one is `MT456169.1`, which is the record the file was copied from.

<!-- nlr-allow: 655 -->

So the two hit lists don't overlap. *Gadus morhua* is absent from all fifty rows
for `mystery_fillet_1`, and *Gadus chalcogrammus* is absent from all fifty rows
for `cod_reference_MT456169`. Those are two fish, and no amount of reading the
sequences by eye would have told you so.

That's the substitution test, and it needs no bench and no permission. What it
can't tell you is who swapped what, or where in the chain it happened. A
sequence identifies tissue. It doesn't assign blame.

One more thing about that table, because you should know where your data came
from. Row eleven is `MN850428.1`, and that's where I got the query. I took a
deposited Alaska pollock barcode, dropped its header, and saved the bases as
`mystery_fillet_1`. So one of the hits is the query itself, which is why it
matched perfectly. Cross that row out and the answer doesn't move. Forty-nine
other records still match, and forty-eight of them carry the same species name.

### The control: same letters, no history

`data/sequences/shuffled_control.fasta` holds 649 bases. Same length as
`mystery_fillet_1`, and the same count of every base, because it is
`mystery_fillet_1` with the order scrambled. Nothing else about it changed. The
shuffle used a fixed number, 20260802, so anybody can regenerate exactly this
file.

Put it through the same form and the same database. Here's the whole result:

``` {.default .output}
Query= shuffled_control

Length=649

No significant similarity found.
```

Zero hits. Against 128,547,243 sequences and 948,086,538,397 letters, a
649-base query came back with nothing worth reporting.

Sit with those two searches side by side. Same length, and the same count of
every base. One of them filled its hit list with fifty records and the other
came back with none. The difference between them is history. One is a piece of an
animal with relatives in the database, and the other is those same letters in an
order no animal has ever carried.

That's what a negative control buys you. Any search that returns hits leaves one
question open: would it have returned hits anyway? You've now watched this form
come back empty, so you know it's capable of saying no.

::: {.check}
The `shuffled_control` report should read `No significant similarity found.`
and `Length=649`. If hits come back, check the first bases of what you pasted.
`shuffled_control` starts `GTCCAATG` and `mystery_fillet_1` starts `CCTTTATC`.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="6.1" time="35 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Identify `mystery_fillet_1` yourself, and write down the evidence rather than
the answer.
:::
::: {.given}
`data/sequences/mystery_fillet_1.fasta`, 649 bases of DNA, no other
information about it.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three things: the species name as two words, the accession of the
highest-scoring hit including its version suffix, and one sentence saying why
more than one record supports the identification.
:::
::: {.check}
Your accession should carry a dot and a number after it. If it doesn't, you
wrote down the record and not the edition, and Chapter 5 says why that matters.
Then test your sentence: delete the top-scoring row from the table and read the
sentence again. If it stops being true, it was a sentence about one record
rather than about the evidence.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="6.2" time="25 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Run the negative control, then say what a search with no hits is telling you.
:::
::: {.given}
`data/sequences/shuffled_control.fasta`, 649 bases, the same base composition
as `mystery_fillet_1`. Before you run anything, write down whether you expect
hits and why.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three items: your written prediction, the result, and which of three readings
applies. Either the sequence is unlike anything deposited, or the query is
too short to reach significance, or the search went against the wrong
database. Name the check that ruled out each of the other two.
:::
::: {.check}
Rule out the wrong database by putting
`data/sequences/cod_reference_MT456169.fasta` through the identical form. That
one is a real Atlantic cod barcode and every hit it returns is *Gadus morhua*,
so a form that answers it is a form that works. Rule out length by comparing:
both queries are 649 bases, and one of them filled its whole hit list, so 649
bases is long enough here. That leaves the first reading, and this is the rare
case where you can be sure of it, because you know where the sequence came from.
For an unknown off a real sample you'd never be that sure.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="7"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

<!-- nlr-allow: 447400 -->

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="The page has been sitting there for minutes and nothing has happened"}
Nothing on your machine is stuck. Your search is in a queue on NCBI's servers,
and the page reloads itself while it waits. Don't press the search button
again: that starts a second job behind the first and slows both of them down.
Write the request ID down before you close anything, because it's how you ask
for that job's results again.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your report is labeled with a species you never asked about"}
You pasted a file whose header names an organism. Pasting a header is allowed,
and BLAST takes it as the query's name without counting it in the length. The
damage is to you, not to the search. Paste `cod_reference_MT456169.fasta` and
the report's query line starts `Query= MT456169.1 Gadus morhua voucher
USNM:FISH:447400` and runs on from there. That line sits directly above a table
of hits from whatever the sequence actually is. Skim it and you'll read your own
label back as the answer. The species you want is in the hit rows, never in the
`Query=` line.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The form refuses your sequence and complains about the characters in it"}
The website is talking, and it's talking before any search has run. The usual
cause is a protein sent to a nucleotide search. Count the different letters in
your sequence. DNA uses four of them and a protein uses twenty. An E, an F, an L
or a Q in there means it isn't DNA. Send a protein query to the protein search
instead. If the sequence really is DNA and it's protein hits you want, that's
`blastx`.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Pick between `blastn`, `blastp` and `blastx` given what a query is made of
  and what you want to compare it against
- Read a BLAST hit table and name the organism the rows agree on
- Explain why many records agreeing is stronger evidence than one top row
- Say what a species name on a database record is evidence of, and what it
  isn't
- Run a negative control and say what its result rules out
- Distinguish three reasons a search comes back with no hits, and name the
  check that separates them
:::
